title: Java Fundamentals
description: The next step after the basics: generics, streams and concurrency.
resumo: Generics make code type-safe: `List<String>`, no casts, never raw types. PECS: `? extends` to read, `? super` to write.
Streams: source → lazy intermediate operations → a terminal operation; sequential by default, single-use.
Shared mutable state needs atomicity and visibility: prefer immutability, then atomic classes and concurrent collections.
Use the atomic methods of concurrent maps (`computeIfAbsent`, `merge`), never check-then-act.
Run independent calls in parallel with `CompletableFuture` — always with your own executor for blocking work, and a timeout.
Parallel streams only for large CPU-bound work with no shared state; never for I/O.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a list of `Object` accepts anything; reading from it needs a cast that can fail at runtime with `ClassCastException`.

**Concept:** generics add a type parameter: `List<String>` accepts only Strings, the compiler checks it, and no cast is needed. Classes and methods can declare their own (`<T>`), with bounds such as `<T extends Comparable<T>>`. Wildcards control what a method accepts: `? extends T` to read (producer), `? super T` to write (consumer) — "PECS".

**How it works:** the types exist only at compile time (type erasure), so `new T()` and `instanceof List<String>` are not possible.
examples.interview_question: What are generics for, and what does "? extends T" mean?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Raw types — `List` without a type parameter. There is no checking, and the error appears far away, at runtime. With the type parameter, the compiler rejects it right away.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** "names of active customers, sorted" written with loops needs a new list, an `if`, a sort call and a lot of noise around the actual idea.

**Concept:** a lambda is a short function such as `x -> x * 2` that implements a functional interface (an interface with one abstract method: `Predicate`, `Function`, `Consumer`...). A method reference like `User::getName` is a shorthand for a lambda. A stream processes a collection as a pipeline: a source, then intermediate operations (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`) and a terminal operation (`toList`, `count`, `collect`).

**How it works:** intermediate operations are lazy: nothing runs until the terminal operation. Streams are sequential by default; `parallelStream()` only pays off with lots of CPU-bound data.
examples.code:
List<String> names = customers.stream()
    .filter(Customer::isActive)     // keep active customers
    .map(Customer::getName)         // Customer -> String
    .sorted()
    .toList();                      // terminal: runs the pipeline (Java 16+)

long vip = customers.stream().filter(c -> c.total() > 1000).count();

Map<String, List<Customer>> byCity = customers.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Customer::getCity));
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal stream operations?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Changing outside state from inside a stream, such as adding to an external list. Let the stream build the result. A stream can also be consumed only once.

subsections.subtitle: Concurrency and Immutability
subsections.description: Race conditions, visibility and thread-safe structures.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a visit counter shows fewer visits than really happened under load, and a shared `HashMap` cache gets corrupted by concurrent requests.

**Concept:** threads share the heap. A race condition happens when an operation like `count++` (read, add, write — three steps) is interleaved between threads. Visibility is the other half: without synchronization, one thread may not see another's write. The tools: immutable objects (shareable with no synchronization — the default choice), atomic classes, `synchronized` or locks, and concurrent collections. `volatile` gives visibility, not atomicity.

**How it works:** prefer immutability; when state must be shared, use an atomic class or a concurrent collection and its atomic methods.
examples.interview_question: When would you choose immutability over explicit synchronization?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Check-then-act on a concurrent map. Each call is thread-safe, but the pair is not: two threads both see "absent" and both put. Use the map's atomic methods.

subsections.subtitle: Executors and CompletableFuture
subsections.description: Running independent work in parallel and combining the results.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a dashboard calls three services one after the other: 300 + 400 + 200 ms. They do not depend on each other, so the page could take 400 ms.

**Concept:** instead of creating threads by hand, use an `ExecutorService`, which reuses threads and limits concurrency. `CompletableFuture` composes asynchronous tasks: `supplyAsync` starts one, `thenCombine` joins two results, `exceptionally` handles failures and `orTimeout` stops endless waits.

**How it works:** always pass your own executor for blocking work. Without it, tasks run on the common ForkJoinPool, which is shared by the whole application and sized to the number of CPUs.
examples.interview_question: How do you run independent calls in parallel and combine the results?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Blocking HTTP calls with `supplyAsync` and no executor. They occupy the common pool, and under load every request — and every parallel stream in the application — waits for a free thread.

subsections.subtitle: Streams: Performance and Pitfalls
subsections.description: When streams help, and when they get in the way.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a stream is used everywhere "because it is modern" — including hot loops, parallel I/O and code that changes shared lists.

**Concept:** streams make code declarative, but they create intermediate objects; in hot loops over small collections a plain `for` can be faster. `parallelStream` uses the common ForkJoinPool: it only pays off with lots of data, CPU-bound work and no shared state. Collectors (`groupingBy`, `counting`, `toMap`) express aggregations clearly.

**How it works:** measure before choosing parallel; for most backend code, sequential streams are the right default.
examples.interview_question: When should you avoid parallel streams?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: I/O inside a parallel stream. Each blocking call holds a common-pool thread, so the whole application's parallel work slows down. Keep it sequential, or use `CompletableFuture` with an I/O executor.

subsections.subtitle: Records, Sealed Types and Pattern Matching

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation: These three features work together for data modeling and are taught in **Object-Oriented Programming**: Immutability and Records (Essentials), Sealed Classes and Pattern Matching (Intermediate) — with one payment example that combines all three.
